quiz_org:1.q: In this electron micrograph of the apical cell surface, what forms the fuzzy outer layer at the arrow?
o: Actin filaments of the terminal web
Dense plaques that anchor keratin filaments
Fused strands of tight junction proteins
quiz_org:1.r: The fuzzy coat outside the plasma membrane is the glycocalyx: saccharides attached to glycolipids, glycoproteins and integrins (p. 227). His practice question on p. 321 names this layer the glycocalyx.
quiz_org:1.alt: Electron micrograph of two adjoining cell apices with a yellow arrow on the fuzzy coat over a surface projection.

quiz_org:10.q: In this diagram of the mitotic cell cycle, what happens during the phase at the arrow?
quiz_org:10.r: The 8 hour phase that follows G1 is S, DNA replication. G1 (25 hours) accumulates enzymes and nucleotides and G2 (2.5 to 3 hours) is preparation for mitosis (p. 246).
quiz_org:10.alt: Circular diagram of the cell cycle with durations; a yellow arrow points to one segment of the outer ring.

quiz_org:11.q: Which protein is made on free ribosomes rather than on the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
quiz_org:11.r: Free ribosomes make cytosolic and cytoskeletal proteins and proteins imported into the nucleus, mitochondria and peroxisomes; rough ER ribosomes make membrane, lysosomal and secreted proteins (p. 251).

quiz_org:12.q: A signal recognition particle binds the signal peptide of a nascent polypeptide. What is the immediate effect?
o: The protein is tagged with ubiquitin
quiz_org:12.r: The signal recognition particle (SRP) inhibits further elongation until the complex binds the SRP receptor on the ER membrane; the signal peptide is removed later, inside the lumen (p. 252).

quiz_org:13.q: Which process takes place in the organelle shown in this electron micrograph?
o: Cleavage of pro-proteins to mature form
quiz_org:13.r: Ribosome-studded cisternae are rough ER, where initial (core) glycosylation of asparagine occurs (p. 261). The other four are Golgi steps (pp. 266-267, 340), which is the point of his practice question on p. 322.
quiz_org:13.alt: Electron micrograph of parallel membrane sacs studded with small dark granules.

quiz_org:14.q: The organelle at the yellow arrow is especially prominent in cells that do what?
quiz_org:14.r: Tubules with no ribosomes are smooth ER, which synthesizes phospholipids, fats and steroids (p. 257) and is prominent in cells that secrete steroid hormones; rough ER is prominent in protein secreting cells (p. 338).
quiz_org:14.alt: Electron micrograph of cytoplasm filled with small branching tubules; a yellow arrow points to them.

quiz_org:15.q: What takes place at the region of this Golgi apparatus marked by the arrow?
o: Receipt of vesicles from the rough ER
quiz_org:15.r: The arrow is on the trans Golgi network, where sorting and secretory vesicle formation occur (pp. 266-267, 324). Vesicles from the ER arrive at the cis face and lysosomal sugars are phosphorylated in the cis Golgi network (p. 266).
quiz_org:15.alt: Electron micrograph of a curved stack of flattened membrane sacs with a yellow arrow at one side of the stack.

quiz_org:16.q: A cell cannot add mannose-6-phosphate in the cis Golgi. Which proteins fail to reach their destination?
quiz_org:16.r: The mannose-6-phosphate marker, added in the cis Golgi, determines segregation to lysosomes (pp. 267, 271).

quiz_org:17.q: How does the organelle at the arrow form?
o: A nascent vesicle buds from the Golgi
It divides by fission from a parent
A primary lysosome fuses with a vesicle
Enzymes are imported from the cytosol
quiz_org:17.r: A membrane sac full of small vesicles is a multivesicular body, a secondary lysosome (p. 323): a primary lysosome fused with another vesicle, organelle or cytoplasmic content (p. 275).
quiz_org:17.alt: Electron micrograph of a large membrane-bound body that contains many small vesicles, marked by a yellow arrow.

quiz_org:18.q: What keeps the interior of a lysosome near pH 5?
o: A proton pump in its membrane
Channel proteins open to the cytosol
quiz_org:18.r: The lysosomal membrane contains a proton pump that maintains the internal pH around 5, the optimum for acid hydrolases, which are largely inactive at cytosolic pH 7.2 (pp. 274, 341).

quiz_org:19.q: A disease of the organelle shown causes which material to accumulate in tissues?
quiz_org:19.r: A crystalline core marks a peroxisome (pp. 279, 325). Adrenoleukodystrophy is a disorder of peroxisomal fatty acid beta oxidation in which very-long-chain fatty acids accumulate (p. 281).
quiz_org:19.alt: Colorized electron micrograph of a round membrane-bound organelle with a dense core.

quiz_org:2.q: The arrow marks where the membranes of two epithelial cells appear to fuse. What does this junction do?
o: Blocks passage of material between cells
Passes ions and sugars from cell to cell
Anchors keratin filaments like a spot weld
Anchors the cell to the basement membrane
quiz_org:2.r: Where adjacent membranes appear to fuse is the zonula occludens (tight junction), a permeability barrier so material cannot pass between cells; it also divides the membrane into apical and basolateral regions (pp. 352-353).
quiz_org:2.alt: Electron micrograph of two adjoining cell apices with a yellow arrow on the apposed lateral membranes.

quiz_org:20.q: What do the knob-like particles on the folds at the arrow do?
o: Make ATP as protons pass through
quiz_org:20.r: The folds are cristae of the inner mitochondrial membrane; their elementary (F1) particles hold ATP synthetase activity and make ATP as protons flow through them (pp. 288-289, 343-344). Citric acid cycle enzymes and calcium granules are in the matrix.
quiz_org:20.alt: Electron micrograph of an oval organelle with many internal folds; a yellow arrow points to the folds.

quiz_org:21.q: This muscle biopsy is from a patient with exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis. Which organelle is defective?
quiz_org:21.r: Ragged red muscle fibers with low energy and lactic acidosis are mitochondrial myopathy (p. 291).
quiz_org:21.alt: Light micrograph of muscle fibers in cross section; some fibers have irregular red-staining rims.

quiz_org:22.q: Which of these cytoplasmic structures is enclosed by a membrane?
quiz_org:22.r: Lipofuscin and melanosomes are membrane enclosed; glycogen, lipid and keratohyaline granules have no membrane (pp. 293, 296).

quiz_org:23.q: Loss of which enzyme activity prevents pigment synthesis in the granules at the arrow?
quiz_org:23.r: The dark granules are melanosomes (p. 294). Albinism is lack of tyrosinase activity, which prevents melanin synthesis in melanosomes (p. 295).
quiz_org:23.alt: Light micrograph of a folded tissue; a yellow arrow points to a cluster of dark granules in one cell layer.

quiz_org:24.q: Which statement about the structures at the arrows is correct?
o: They are bounded by two membranes
They contain their own circular DNA
quiz_org:24.r: Lipid droplets in electron micrographs show a dark perimeter but are not bound by a membrane (pp. 301, 345).
quiz_org:24.alt: Electron micrograph of cytoplasm; yellow arrows point to round, evenly gray bodies with dark edges.

quiz_org:25.q: The filaments of the layer at the arrow attach to which junction?
quiz_org:25.r: The layer under the microvilli is the terminal web: actin filaments attached to the zonula adherens, into which the actin of microvilli and stereocilia anchors (p. 307).
quiz_org:25.alt: Electron micrograph of finger-like apical projections; a yellow arrow points to the layer beneath their bases.

quiz_org:26.q: What best describes the stereocilia of the epididymis?
quiz_org:26.r: Stereocilia are held up by non-contractile bundles of actin filaments, like microvilli; in the epididymis they aid absorption (pp. 306, 351).

quiz_org:27.q: Where, besides the centrosome, is a structure with this microtubule arrangement found?
quiz_org:27.r: Nine triplets of microtubules is a centriole (p. 326). A basal body is a centriole at the base of a cilium that nucleates the axoneme; the axoneme itself is doublets and forms the core of cilia and the sperm tail (pp. 312, 348).
quiz_org:27.alt: Electron micrograph of a ring of grouped microtubules cut in cross section.

quiz_org:28.q: In a motile cilium, what generates the sliding force between adjacent microtubule doublets?
quiz_org:28.r: Dynein arms on one doublet interact with the adjacent doublet and hydrolyze ATP to generate a sliding force, which is converted into bending (p. 349).

quiz_org:29.q: Which filaments insert into the plaques of the junction at the arrow?
quiz_org:29.r: The junction is a desmosome: keratin filaments attach to desmosomes to form a framework in the cytoplasm (p. 318), and desmosomes act like spot welds that anchor keratin filaments (p. 353).
quiz_org:29.alt: Diagram of epithelial cells with red filaments and blue plaques; a yellow arrow points to a paired plaque between two cells.

quiz_org:3.q: Which pair consists only of organelles enclosed by two membranes?
quiz_org:3.r: Each mitochondrion has a double membrane (p. 285) and the nuclear envelope has an inner and an outer membrane (p. 229). Peroxisomes have a single membrane (p. 342).

quiz_org:4.q: A mutation in a protein of the blue meshwork at the arrow causes which disease?
quiz_org:4.r: The meshwork under the inner nuclear membrane is the nuclear lamina, made of lamins, which are intermediate filaments (p. 230). Progeria is linked to a mutation in the lamin A gene (p. 231).
quiz_org:4.alt: Diagram of the nuclear envelope between cytosol and nucleus with a yellow arrow on a blue meshwork.

quiz_org:5.q: What is made in the dark round body marked by the arrows?
quiz_org:5.r: The dark body inside the nucleus is the nucleolus, which makes ribosomal RNA (pp. 235-236). No protein synthesis occurs in the nucleus (p. 330).
quiz_org:5.alt: Light micrograph of large pale cells; yellow arrows point to a dark round body inside each nucleus.

quiz_org:6.q: In this electron micrograph of a nucleus, what describes the dark material at the yellow arrow?
quiz_org:6.r: Dark clumps against the nuclear envelope are heterochromatin: highly condensed, generally inactive DNA. Euchromatin is light staining, uncoiled and transcriptionally active (pp. 242, 330).
quiz_org:6.alt: Electron micrograph of a whole nucleus with a yellow arrow on a dark clump at its edge.

quiz_org:7.q: Which region of the nucleolus contains the maturing ribosomal subunits?
quiz_org:7.r: Pars amorpha (nucleolar organizer) is the DNA coding for rRNA, pars fibrosa is the primary rRNA transcripts, and pars granulosa is the maturing ribosomal subunits (pp. 237-238).

quiz_org:8.q: Which feature do archaea share with eukaryotes but not with bacteria?
quiz_org:8.r: Archaea glycosylate proteins whereas bacteria do not, which is evidence that archaea were the host cell; archaea are still prokaryotes with no organelles (pp. 220, 224).

quiz_org:9.q: Which organelle divides by the process shown in column A?
quiz_org:9.r: Column A is binary fission, the prokaryote mechanism that gives clones; the slide adds that mitochondria and chloroplasts divide this way too (p. 245), and new mitochondria arise by fission, not mitosis (p. 285).
quiz_org:9.alt: Diagram of three ways a cell can divide, in columns labeled A, B and C.

quiz_org_b:1.q: According to the lecture's account of organelle biogenesis, how did mitochondria arise?
quiz_org_b:1.r: Endosymbiosis of eubacteria, which became mitochondria and chloroplasts, with an archaebacterial host formed eukaryotic cells; infolding of the plasma membrane formed the other organelles (p. 224).

quiz_org_b:2.q: A straight cytoskeletal element in an electron micrograph measures 25 nm across. By the lecture's diameters, what is it?
quiz_org_b:2.r: Microtubules are 25 nm in diameter; microfilaments (actin) are 5-7 nm and intermediate filaments, which include keratin, are 8-10 nm (p. 303).

quiz_org_b:3.q: An organelle generates hydrogen peroxide and uses it to oxidize harmful substances such as alcohol. Which organelle is it?
quiz_org_b:3.r: Peroxisomes generate hydrogen peroxide, which oxidizes harmful substances; they detoxify alcohol and carry out the first step of beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids (p. 280).

brief:
Cell Organelles High-Yield Tables (Exam 3)

Cell Organelles and Cell Specializations (Djakiew) has not been quizzed yet, so every topic is covered evenly. Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF: slides pp. 214–327, handout pp. 328–355. Everything is from those pages unless labeled (outside the slides). The "In an image" columns are my descriptions of his pictures; the slides give only titles and labels.

1. Prokaryotes, eukaryotes and cell division (LO 3)

Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have no organelles and divide by binary fission; eukaryotes have organelles and divide by mitosis or meiosis (pp. 220, 245).

Milestone When What made it possible Page
Prokaryotes 3.7 billion years past Prebiotic origin of life 219
Eukaryotes 2.5 billion years past Endosymbiosis (Lynn Margulis) 219
Metazoans At least 1 billion years past Cell junctions and connective tissue, needed for multicellularity 219
Homeotic (Hox) gene family At least 600 million years past Segmentation morphogenesis 219
Tissue differentiation and organogenesis At least 600 million years past Specialized organ systems 219
Domain Organelles Notes Page
Bacteria (eubacteria) None Photosynthesis releases oxygen 220, 223
Archaea None DNA with introns, promoters and histones; glycosylate proteins 220, 224
Eukaryotes Present Appear 2.5 billion years past 220, 223

Stromatolites are 3.7 billion year old fossils; living ones are mats of mostly cyanobacteria that deposit calcium carbonate (p. 221). The Last Universal Common Ancestor coincides with the Great Oxidation Event (p. 223).

How eukaryotes arose (p. 224) Detail
Endosymbiosis Eubacteria became mitochondria and chloroplasts inside an archaeal host
Infolding of plasma membrane Wrapped clusters of proteins and enzymes to form discrete organelles
Nucleus Most likely from an archaeal progenitor: archaea have introns, promoters, histones and eukaryote-like RNA polymerase
Glycosylation Archaea glycosylate proteins, bacteria do not: more evidence that archaea were the host
Feature Prokaryote Eukaryote Page
Nucleus None Present; separates transcription from translation 328
Organelles None Present 220
Division Binary fission; gives clones Mitosis; meiosis gives genetic diversity 245
Also divide this way Mitochondria and chloroplasts 245
Evidence that mitochondria were prokaryotes (p. 285)
Same size as bacteria
Own small circular DNA chromosome, ribosomes, messenger RNA and transfer RNA, all like bacterial ones
New mitochondria arise by fission from existing ones, not by mitosis
Double membrane: outer from the host cell, inner from the symbiotic prokaryote
Closest relatives by genotyping are the rickettsia bacteria

One conflict: the slide says aerobic bacteria gave rise to mitochondria and names rickettsia as the closest relatives (pp. 284–285), while the handout says a purple photosynthetic bacterium (p. 342). Answer with the handout wording unless a question quotes the slide's "closest relatives".

Cell cycle phase Duration on the slide What happens Page
G1 25 hours Accumulate enzymes and nucleotides 246
S 8 hours DNA replication 246
G2 2.5–3 hours Preparation for mitosis 246
M (mitosis) Prophase about 1 hour, metaphase under 1 hour, anaphase under half an hour, telophase minutes Division 246

Interphase is G1, S and G2 together: the period of growth between mitoses when the cell carries out its normal functions (pp. 246–247).

Mitosis phase What happens (p. 247)
Prophase Nucleus disappears; chromatin condenses into chromosomes; centrosomes move to opposite poles and form the spindle
Metaphase Chromosomes condense further and align at the equatorial plane
Anaphase Sister chromosomes move toward the spindle poles
Telophase Sister chromosomes arrive at the poles
Cytokinesis A cleavage furrow divides cytoplasm and chromosomes into two daughter cells
Cell cycle link Detail Page
Nuclear envelope breakdown Lamina proteins are phosphorylated just before and during mitosis 328
Chromosome condensation Thought to start with phosphorylation of a histone 332
Nucleolus Disassembles in mitosis; up to 10 form right after, then fuse into one 239, 329
Mitotic spindle Microtubules nucleated by the centrosomes 312
Cleavage furrow Contractile ring of actin and myosin under the membrane 351

2. Plasma membrane (LO 2)

The plasma membrane is a lipid bilayer with proteins in and on it and a sugar coat outside (p. 227).

Part What it is Function In an image
Lipid bilayer Phospholipids: charged, polar heads; non-polar fatty acid tails inside Barrier Thin dark line bounding the cell (p. 226)
Integral (transmembrane) proteins Span the bilayer Pores and receptors
Peripheral (extrinsic) proteins Sit on the surface Accessory proteins
Glycocalyx Sugars on glycolipids, glycoproteins and integrins, on the exterior Cell coat Fuzzy layer on the outer surface (p. 321)
Freeze fracture faces External (E) face and protoplasmic (P) face

3. The list: which structures have a membrane (LO 1)

The overview drawing names lysosome, mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum, peroxisome, ribosomes, secretory granules, vesicles, nucleus, Golgi apparatus and nucleolus (pp. 228, 248); the cell specializations in the objectives are microvilli, cell junctions, inclusions and cytoskeleton (p. 218).

Structure Membrane Page
Nucleus Two: inner and outer, with a cisterna between 229, 328
Mitochondrion Two: outer and inner (folded into cristae) 285, 342
Endoplasmic reticulum One continuous membrane around one lumen 337
Golgi apparatus Stack of membrane cisternae 263, 340
Lysosome Yes; holds a proton pump 341
Peroxisome Single membrane 342
Melanosome Membrane enclosed 293
Lipofuscin Membrane enclosed 293
Glycogen No membrane 293, 296
Lipid droplet No membrane 293, 301
Keratohyaline granule No membrane; in the stratum granulosum 296

One conflict: the slides call melanosomes membrane enclosed (pp. 293, 296); the handout says they have a membrane when first formed and may lose it as they mature (p. 344). Answer "membrane bound" unless a question asks about mature melanosomes.

4. Nucleus (LO 2)

The nucleus separates transcription from translation so that messenger RNA can be processed before it reaches the cytoplasm (p. 328).

Part Structure Function In an image
Outer membrane Continuous with rough endoplasmic reticulum; may carry ribosomes Extension of the rough endoplasmic reticulum Outer of two lines (pp. 229–230)
Cisterna (perinuclear space) Space between the two membranes
Inner membrane Lacks ribosomes; joins the outer membrane at the pores Binds the lamina
Nuclear lamina Meshwork of lamins A, B and C (intermediate filaments) under the inner membrane Binds chromatin; gives the nucleus its shape Blue meshwork in the diagram; fibrous net in the micrograph (p. 230)
Nuclear pore complex Nucleoporins with eightfold symmetry; about 50 proteins; 3,000–4,000 pores per nucleus Regulates movement of macromolecules Small rings on the envelope in the drawing (p. 229)
Nucleolus Dark staining region Makes ribosomal RNA (rRNA) Dark round body inside the nucleus (p. 235)
Heterochromatin Condensed; often against the envelope except at pores Generally inactive DNA Heavy staining, dark clumps (pp. 241–242)
Euchromatin Uncoiled Transcriptionally active Light staining, pale (pp. 241–242)

Pages: 229–230, 233, 236, 240, 328–330.

Nuclear pore traffic Detail Page
Small ions and solutes Simple diffusion through the channel 234
Size limit for free passage Particles smaller than 9 nm 329
Outbound Ribosomal subunits and other RNA-associated proteins 234
Inbound Chromatin proteins, ribosomal proteins, transcription factors, enzymes 234
Signals Nuclear import and export sequences bind importins and exportins 233
Energy Import is energy dependent 329
Nucleolus region Contains Page
Nucleolar organizer (pars amorpha) DNA coding for rRNA; pale staining 237, 329
Pars fibrosa Primary rRNA transcripts; fine 5 nm fibers 237, 330
Pars granulosa Maturing ribosomal subunits; 15 nm granules 237, 330
Nucleolus-associated chromatin Function unknown 238
Nucleolonema Pars fibrosa plus pars granulosa, without the pars amorpha 238

Nucleolus size is directly related to the synthetic activity of the cell (p. 329). Ribosomal proteins are made in the cytoplasm and imported, because no protein synthesis occurs in the nucleus (p. 330).

Chromatin packing step Size on the slide Page
DNA double helix 2 nm 243
Nucleosomes, "beads on a string": DNA around 8 histones 11 nm 243, 331
Chromatin fiber 30 nm 243, 332
Looped domains 300 nm 243
Condensed chromosome 700 nm 243
Metaphase chromosome 1400 nm 243
Chromatin and genome fact Detail Page
Components DNA, histones, non-histone proteins (transcription factors) 240
Histones Small, highly positive, 5 types, highly conserved 331
Human chromosomes 46 in a diploid nucleus; 24 different kinds 330
Genome 3.2 billion base pairs; about 30,000 genes; 1–2% codes for protein or RNA 331
DNA methylation On some cytosines; copied by maintenance methylase; genomic imprinting 331
Transcription factor families Zinc fingers; leucine zippers (form heterodimers) 333
Messenger RNA processing step Detail Page
First transcript Heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA) 333
Cap 7-methyl guanosine; signal for ribosome attachment 333
Poly A tail About 200 adenylate residues 334
Splicing Small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) in a spliceosome remove introns; exons stay 334
Alternative splicing One hnRNA gives different proteins 334
Share that leaves Only 5% of the RNA mass ever leaves the nucleus 333

5. Ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum (LO 2)

Where a ribosome sits decides where its protein goes: free ribosomes make proteins that stay in the cytosol or are imported, bound ribosomes make proteins that enter the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (p. 251).

Ribosome fact Detail Page
Structure Small and large subunit joined on a messenger RNA (mRNA) strand; 25 nm 249
Made in Nucleolus 336
Staining Intensely basophilic (hematoxylin) because of RNA 336
Activity Ribozyme: RNA does the enzymatic work 336
Polysome One mRNA with many ribosomes 336
Roles mRNA specifies the sequence; transfer RNA (tRNA) ferries amino acids 250
Ribosome location Makes Page
Free Cytosolic and cytoskeletal proteins; proteins imported into nucleus, mitochondria and peroxisomes 251
Bound to rough ER Proteins for membranes, lysosomes or secretion 251
Entry into the rough ER (RER), in order Page
Signal peptide (20–25 hydrophobic amino acids) emerges 337
Signal recognition particle (SRP) binds it and stops elongation 252
Complex binds the SRP receptor (docking protein) on the ER membrane 252, 337
SRP releases; translation continues through a translocator (vectorial discharge) 252, 337
Signal peptidase removes the signal peptide inside the lumen 252, 258
ER type Structure Functions Prominent in In an image
Rough Flattened sacs (cisternae); ribosomes on the cytoplasmic side only Signal peptide cleavage, protein folding, attachment of oligosaccharides, disulfide bonds Protein secreting cells Parallel sacs studded with dark dots (pp. 255, 322)
Smooth Fine tubules, no ribosomes Makes phospholipids, fats, steroids and cholesterol; detoxifies drugs; breaks down glycogen; stores and releases calcium for muscle contraction Cells secreting steroid hormones Branching tubules with no dots (p. 256)
Transitional Ribosome-free region next to rough ER Transfer vesicles pinch off

Pages: 257, 338–339. The ER is visible only by electron microscopy and its lumen may be 10% of cell volume (p. 337).

RER processing fact Detail Page
Folding Chaperone proteins pull the chain into the lumen; it folds on release 258
Core glycosylation Sugars built on dolichol (a lipid) through a pyrophosphate link, then moved to asparagine: N-linked 261
Misfolded protein Sent back to the cytosol, tagged with ubiquitin, degraded by proteasomes 258

6. Golgi apparatus (LO 2)

The Golgi modifies, sorts and packages proteins from the ER, and microtubules hold it in shape (p. 263).

Golgi level, cis to trans What happens there Page
Cis (forming) face Receives vesicles budding from the rough ER 263, 340
Cis Golgi network Phosphorylation of oligosaccharides on lysosomal proteins (mannose-6-phosphate added) 266–267
Cis cisterna Removal of mannose 266
Medial cisterna Removal of mannose; addition of N-acetylglucosamine 266
Trans cisterna Addition of galactose 266
Trans Golgi network Addition of N-acetylneuraminic acid; sorting; secretory vesicle formation 266, 324
Trans (maturing) face Condensing and secretory vesicles; often faces the plasma membrane 263, 340

Golgi enzymes carry out glycosylation, sulfation, phosphorylation and limited proteolysis (p. 266). In an image the Golgi is a curved stack of about 6 flattened cisternae with vesicles at both faces (pp. 264, 324, 340).

Transport signal Role Page
Coat protein II (COP-II) Forward movement, ER to Golgi 265
Coat protein I (COP-I) Retrograde movement, Golgi back to ER 265
KDEL receptor Retrieves misfolded proteins from the Golgi back to the ER 265
Mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) Added in the cis Golgi; sends proteins to lysosomes 267, 271
v-SNAREs On transfer vesicles; decide what the vesicle fuses with 339
pH Neutral in the ER, more acidic toward the trans Golgi 265
Route out of the trans Golgi network (p. 267) Signal needed
To lysosomes Yes: mannose-6-phosphate receptor
Regulated secretion in secretory vesicles Yes
Constitutive secretion to the cell surface No

Larger vesicles may be secreted from endocrine cells; smaller ones, such as synaptic vesicles, travel down microtubules (p. 268).

7. Lysosomes and peroxisomes (LO 2)

Lysosomes digest with acid hydrolases at pH 5; peroxisomes oxidize with hydrogen peroxide (pp. 274, 280).

Lysosome type Definition In an image Page
Primary Nascent vesicle budded from the Golgi Small, homogeneous 275, 341
Secondary Primary lysosome fused with another vesicle, organelle or cytoplasmic content Mixed contents; a sac full of small vesicles is a multivesicular body 275, 323
Tertiary Remnant of digestion: residual body, lipofuscin 275
Secondary lysosome kind Contents Page
Digestive vacuole Phagocytosed large particles such as bacteria 342
Autophagic vacuole The cell's own organelles, such as mitochondria 342
Multivesicular body Numerous vesicles 342

One conflict: the slides make the residual body and lipofuscin a tertiary lysosome (pp. 275, 293), while the handout files residual bodies and lipofuscin under secondary lysosomes (pp. 341, 344). His own practice question on p. 323 lists "tertiary lysosome", "residual body" and "lipofuscin body" as choices separate from "secondary lysosome", so here use the slide's three classes.

Lysosome fact Detail Page
Enzymes Acid hydrolases: nucleases, proteases, glycosidases, lipases, phosphatases, sulfatases, phospholipases 274
pH Optimal at pH 5; largely inactive at cytosolic pH 7.2 274
How pH is kept Proton pump in the lysosomal membrane 341
Why it matters Protects the cytoplasm if enzymes leak 341
Size 0.05–0.5 micrometers 274
Origin Trans Golgi network 341
Light microscope Dark granules in the cytoplasm 272
Endocytosis types Phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated endocytosis 277
Peroxisome fact Detail Page
Structure Oxidative enzymes in a single membrane 342
In an image Round body with a crystalline core 279, 325
Reaction Generates hydrogen peroxide, which oxidizes harmful substances; catalase uses it 280, 342
Detoxifies Alcohol and other harmful chemicals 280
Fatty acids Beta oxidation of long-chain fatty acids, the first step of their catabolism 280
Proteins Imported selectively from the cytoplasm 342

8. Mitochondria (LO 2)

Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP and soak up excess cytoplasmic calcium (p. 290).

Part Contains Page
Outer membrane Channel-forming proteins; permeable to small molecules 342
Intermembrane space Like cytosol for small molecules; protons are pumped into it 342–343
Inner membrane Impermeable to ions; folded into cristae; holds the electron transport chain and transport proteins 343
Elementary (F1) particles Knobs on the inner membrane with ATP synthetase activity 287–288, 343
Matrix Citric acid cycle enzymes; DNA, mRNA, tRNA, ribosomes; dense calcium granules 343

In an electron micrograph a mitochondrion is an oval body with a double membrane and internal folds, the cristae (pp. 286–287); by fluorescence it is a thread-like network that co-localizes with the cytoskeleton (p. 283).

Making ATP, in order Page
The citric acid cycle makes NADH in the matrix 343
The electron transport chain passes electrons to oxygen and pumps protons into the intermembrane space 343
Protons flow back through the elementary particle and spin its rotor 289, 344
The rotation drives synthesis of ATP from ADP and phosphate 289, 344

The slide says elementary particles "act as proton pumps that facilitate the synthesis of ATP" (p. 288); the handout says protons pass through the F1 particle and it makes ATP (p. 344). Both agree the particle is where ATP is made.

Mitochondria fact Detail Page
Yield 36 ATP aerobic; 2 ATP anaerobic 290
Calcium Sequester excess cytoplasmic calcium; damaged mitochondria release it 290
Inheritance Maternal: few if any sperm mitochondria remain in the zygote 286
DNA 37 genes, about 16,000 base pairs 286
Mitochondrial Eve Matrilineal common ancestor, about 190,000–200,000 years ago 286
Number Most numerous in cells needing much energy 342
Three-parent in vitro fertilization Removes defective mitochondrial DNA 292

9. Cytoplasmic inclusions (LO 1 and LO 2)

Pigment granules have a membrane; glycogen, lipid and keratohyaline granules do not (pp. 293, 296).

Inclusion Membrane What it is In an image Page
Melanosome Yes Granule containing melanin Dark granules, shown in the pigmented layer of the retina 293–294
Lipofuscin Yes Lipid-containing residue of lysosomal digestion; residual body, tertiary lysosome 293
Glycogen No Branched glucose polymer; energy store in liver and muscle Stains with periodic acid-Schiff; small dense irregular granules by electron microscopy 296, 345
Lipid No Triglycerides in storage form Round droplets with a dark perimeter by electron microscopy; lost in routine sections, so they look empty 299, 301, 345
Keratohyaline granule No In the stratum granulosum 296

Slide 297 (magenta-stained liver cells) and slide 300 (fat cells) have no captions; from their position I read them as glycogen and lipid examples. Lipid needs frozen sections and a fat soluble dye, or osmium fixation (p. 345).

10. Cytoskeleton (LO 2)

Three filament systems, told apart by diameter, subunit and stability (pp. 303, 346).

Filament Diameter Subunit Behavior Page
Microfilament 5–7 nm Actin: globular G-actin forms a double helix of filamentous F-actin Very dynamic 303–304, 349
Intermediate filament 8–10 nm Fibrous proteins that differ by cell type Stable; resists mechanical stress 303, 346–347
Microtubule 25 nm Heterodimer of alpha and beta tubulin Polar; grows and shrinks at one end preferentially 303, 311, 347

Diameters differ slightly in the handout: microfilaments 5 nm and intermediate filaments 7 to 11 nm (p. 346). Give the handout numbers unless a question quotes the slide.

12. Cell junctions and adhesion molecules (LO 2)

The slides say cell junctions were needed for multicellular life (p. 219); the handout gives four junctions, listed in its figure as zonula occludens, zonula adherens, desmosome, gap junction (p. 352).

Junction Shape and look Filament or protein Function Page
Zonula occludens (tight junction) Membranes appear to fuse; strands of particles on freeze fracture Calcium dependent proteins Blocks passage between cells; separates apical from basolateral membrane 352–353
Zonula adherens (intermediate junction, belt desmosome) Continuous band around the apex; two plaques Actin filaments; cadherins Attaches actin to the membrane; transmits contractile force 353–354
Desmosome (macula adherens) Button-like; two dense plaques 20 nm apart, often with a dense central line Keratin filaments; calcium dependent proteins Spot weld; anchors keratin 318, 353
Hemidesmosome Half a desmosome on the basal surface Keratin filaments (diagram) Anchors the cell to the basement membrane 318, 353
Gap (communicating) junction Membranes 2 nm apart; hundreds of connexons, each of 6 connexins Connexin Passes ions, sugars and amino acids; electrical coupling in heart and smooth muscle 352

The gap junction is the most common type of junction (p. 352). Similar structures to the zonula adherens occur in the intercalated disks of heart muscle (p. 353).
